corpus_definition: To have enough money to buy something.

forms.definition: how cheap something is, so that people have enough money for it
forms.example: The affordability of flats in Tashkent is a big problem for young families.

syn.note: Cheapness is about a low price; the longer word is about whether normal people can pay.

forms.definition: to have enough money to pay for something
forms.example: We can't afford a new car this year.
forms.note: Usually with can, could or be able to: 'I can't afford it.' Also afford + to do: 'We can't afford to wait.'

syn.note: Easy everyday phrase; 'can pay for' is close, but afford stresses having enough money.
Informal: 'Can you manage 100,000 sum?' means 'Do you have enough money for it?'
To spare money is to give some because you have enough: 'Can you spare 10 dollars?'

forms.definition: cheap enough for most people to buy
forms.example: The new shop sells good, affordable clothes for students.

syn.note: Easy word; cheap can also mean 'low quality', the longer word is always positive.
Very close and a little formal.
A reasonable price is fair, not too high.

ant.note: Too expensive for most people to buy.

forms.definition: at a price that most people can pay
forms.example: The hotel is clean and affordably priced.
forms.note: Not very common; mostly in the phrase 'affordably priced'.

syn.note: Easy word; cheaply can also suggest low quality.

ant.note: In a way that costs a lot of money.

context.text: My brother could not afford to live near his work. Last month he finally found an affordable flat in Chilonzor, close to the metro.

reviewer_note: afford is almost always used with can/could/be able to; no affix claimed on affordability (-ity leaves no clean word).

gate_overrides.reason: unaffordable is an adjective in the Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries ('too expensive for people to buy'); it is only missing from WordNet 3.1. Opposite of affordable per rule 3.

corpus_definition: quick to notice danger; a warning of possible danger

forms.definition: a warning that something dangerous may happen
forms.example: The city sent a storm alert to everyone's phone.
forms.note: Phrase: on (the) alert = ready to deal with danger.

syn.note: Easy, very close word.
An alarm is often a loud sound or bell that warns people.

forms.definition: the state of being quick to notice and react to things
forms.example: Drivers need alertness, especially at night.

syn.note: Attention is looking or listening carefully; the longer word adds being ready to act.
Awareness is knowing what is happening around you.

forms.definition: to warn someone about a danger or problem
forms.example: A neighbour alerted the police when she saw the smoke.

syn.note: Easy, very close word.
To inform is just to tell someone facts; it does not have to be about danger.
General easy word for giving information.

forms.definition: quick to notice things, especially danger, and ready to act
forms.example: The guard stayed alert throughout the whole night.

syn.note: Watching carefully for problems.
Paying careful attention, often to people.
Easy word: not sleeping. You can be awake but not ready to notice danger.
Easy word: thinking about what you do so nothing bad happens.

ant.note: Tired and slow to notice things.
Not knowing what is happening around you.

forms.note: alertly exists but is very rare; people say 'in an alert way' or 'carefully'.

context.text: The night guard stayed alert and saw smoke coming from a shop. He quickly alerted the fire service, and his alertness saved the whole street.

reviewer_note: Corpus definition mixes adjective and noun; one map with the adjective as base and the noun/verb as conversions.

corpus_definition: a narrow street or path between or behind buildings

forms.definition: a narrow street or path between or behind buildings
forms.example: They walked through a dark alley to reach the market.
forms.note: Plural: alleys.

syn.note: A narrow road, often in the countryside or an old town.
A narrow way through or between places, often inside a building.
Easy word: a narrow way for walking, not always between buildings.
Easy word: any road in a town; usually wider than an alley.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.
There is no adjective made from this word.
There is no adverb made from this word.

context.text: The old part of Bukhara has many narrow alleys. We walked down a quiet alley and found a small tea house.

reviewer_note: Compounds (alleyway, bowling alley) left out for the Compounds branch.

corpus_definition: Next to or together with someone or something.
usage_note: alongside + noun/pronoun: 'He worked alongside his father.' 'The road runs alongside the river.' Also an adverb at the end: 'A car pulled up alongside.'

relations.note: Easy phrase for working or doing something with someone.
Easy phrase for position: very close, at the side.
At the side of; used for position, not for working together.
Simple general word; alongside adds the idea of side by side, as equals.

context.text: My uncle worked alongside his father in the family bakery for many years. Now his son works alongside him every morning.

reviewer_note: kind corrected from word to function (preposition/adverb); no word forms.

corpus_definition: to make a change to something so it is different

forms.definition: a change made to something, such as a plan or clothes
forms.example: We made a few alterations to the plan.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
A small change to make something work or fit better.
Formal; often a change to a machine or a design.

forms.definition: to make something different in some way
forms.example: We need to alter the plan slightly.
forms.note: A little more formal than change. Don't confuse with altar (a table in a church), which sounds the same.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; alter is a little more formal.
To change something a little so it works or fits better.
Formal; often used for machines, plans and designs.
To change something so it fits a new situation.

forms.definition: changed so that it is different from before
forms.example: She came back from the trip with an altered view of the city.

syn.note: Easy, very close word.
Easy word: not the same, but not always because of a change.

ant.note: Easy, common word: staying the same.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from this word.
forms.not_family_note: alternate comes from the same old Latin root (alter = other) but is not made from this word.

context.text: Heavy snow made us alter our travel plans. Because of the alteration, we arrived in Samarkand one day late.

reviewer_note: Homophone trap alter/altar noted; alternate kept out as not_family.

corpus_definition: a senior official sent by a country to represent it abroad

forms.definition: an important official who represents their country in another country
forms.example: The ambassador met the president yesterday.
forms.note: Also used for a famous person who represents a brand or idea: 'a UNICEF goodwill ambassador'.

syn.note: Any official who works for their country abroad; the ambassador is the most senior one.
Formal: a person sent with a special message or job.
A person who speaks or acts for a group, company or country.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.
ambassadorial exists but is rare and formal.
There is no adverb made from this word.

people_not_family_note: embassy (the ambassador's office) shares an old root but is not made from ambassador.

context.text: The British ambassador visited a school in Tashkent last week. The students asked the ambassador many questions about studying abroad.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry; no affix claimed (ambassad- is not a word).

corpus_definition: Something that makes you smile or laugh.

forms.definition: the feeling you have when something is funny
forms.example: She looked at the puppy with amusement.

syn.note: Easy word: enjoyment and pleasure from doing something.
Shows, films and games that people enjoy.
The feeling of liking something; not always about laughing.

ant.note: The feeling when nothing is interesting.

forms.definition: to make someone smile or laugh
forms.example: The clown amused the children for an hour.

syn.note: To keep people interested and happy, for example with a show.
Easy phrase: 'make someone laugh'.
To make someone very happy, not only by being funny.

ant.note: To make someone feel tired and not interested.

forms.definition: making you smile or laugh
forms.example: We watched an amusing film last night.

syn.note: Easy, very common word with the same meaning.
Interesting and enjoyable, not always funny.
A little formal; often about stories and writing.

forms.definition: showing that you think something is funny
forms.example: My teacher gave me an amused smile.
forms.note: amusing = the thing makes you laugh; amused = how you feel.

forms.definition: in a way that makes people smile or laugh
forms.example: He talked amusingly about his first day at work.

syn.note: A little formal, close in meaning.

context.text: My grandfather told us an amusing story about his school days in Fergana. We were all very amused, and even my little sister laughed.

reviewer_note: -ing/-ed trap: amusing (causes the feeling) vs amused (has the feeling); amusement park left out as a compound.

corpus_definition: something that is from a very long time ago

forms.note: Only in the literary phrase 'the ancients' (people who lived very long ago, e.g. the Greeks).
There is no verb made from this word.

forms.definition: from a time very long ago, often thousands of years ago
forms.example: We visited ancient ruins during our summer holiday.
forms.note: Also used jokingly for something just very old: 'My phone is ancient!'

syn.note: Easy, general word; the headword means much older.
Important in history, but not always very old.
Used for old furniture, jewellery and objects that are valuable.
From the time before people wrote history.

ant.note: Of the present time or recent times.
Easy word: made or started recently.

forms.note: anciently exists but is very rare; people say 'in ancient times' or 'long ago'.

context.text: Samarkand is an ancient city on the Silk Road. Every year, tourists come to see its ancient mosques and colourful markets.

reviewer_note: Only one existing form; the ancients and anciently mentioned in notes as rare/literary.

corpus_definition: A public statement about something important to everyone.

forms.definition: a public statement that tells people about something important
forms.example: The school made an important announcement today.

syn.note: Something said or written officially; a little more general.
Formal and official, often about a decision.
Usually written on paper or a board, not spoken.
Easy word: new information about recent events.

forms.definition: to tell people something officially and publicly
forms.example: The airline announced a delay to our flight.

syn.note: Formal; often used for official decisions.
To say something clearly and formally.
Easy word: give information to someone, not always publicly.
To give information about something that happened, often in the news.

forms.note: There is no common adjective; unannounced (without warning) is the opposite idea.
There is no adverb made from this word.

people.definition: a person who reads news or introduces programmes on radio or TV
people.example: The announcer said the train was ten minutes late.

context.text: The head teacher announced the exam dates this morning. After the announcement, the students in our class started to plan their revision.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ment noun; verb announce is the base of the family. unannounced mentioned only in a note.

corpus_definition: To make someone feel a little angry or impatient.

forms.definition: the feeling of being a little angry or impatient
forms.example: To my annoyance, the bus was late again.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.
Easy word, but much stronger.

forms.definition: to make someone feel a little angry or impatient
forms.example: Please stop tapping your pen, it annoys me.

syn.note: Very close; a little more formal.
Easy word; can also mean to disturb someone.
To make someone sad or worried, not only angry.
To make someone very angry; much stronger.

forms.definition: making you feel a little angry or impatient
forms.example: That noise is really annoying.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.
Making you angry because you can't do what you want.

forms.definition: a little angry or impatient about something
forms.example: My mum was annoyed because I came home late.
forms.note: annoying = the thing causes the feeling; annoyed = how you feel. Pattern: annoyed with someone, annoyed about something.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.
Easy word, but stronger.

forms.definition: in a way that makes you feel a little angry
forms.example: The music was annoyingly loud.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.

context.text: The neighbour's dog barks every night, and it really annoys my father. He says the noise is annoying, but he tries not to look annoyed.

reviewer_note: -ing/-ed trap: annoying (causes the feeling) vs annoyed (has the feeling).
